items.label: f02-rubric
items.front: Rubric for accepting the update-guard change (helper imported at src/context/AppDataContext.tsx:27): what must be true, and which patches are rejected?
items.back: Every update callback uses the same helper (1 import + 6 calls), valid replacement preserves order, missing identity throws before any await, add/delete unchanged, tests import production source. Reject patches that insert a missing update, convert update to add, or catch the error and report success.

items.label: f03-screen-reimplements-map
items.front: Finding F2: SaleFormScreen.tsx:97-99 rebuilds nextSales with sales.map((sale) => sale.id === nextSale.id ? nextSale : sale). Why is it flagged even though it is harmless today?
items.back: It re-implements the old silent map in the screen. It is safe only because updateSale already threw for a missing id; it duplicates the policy the helper was meant to own, so a future change can drift.

items.label: f04-derived-status
items.front: One fix direction for the two-write sale save is to stop persisting a derived status. What already derives sold_out (src/utils/calculations.ts:312)?
items.back: The display calculation derives status from quantity: closed stays closed, a current quantity of 0 shows sold_out, otherwise the stored status. If display already derives it, the second updatePigBatch write - and its partial-failure window - could be dropped.

items.label: f01-existence-invariant
items.front: What does replaceRecordById (src/utils/collection.ts:1-8) do for a match, for a missing id, and what boundary does it make explicit?
items.back: Match: returns a new array with every record of that id replaced. Missing: throws 'Record <id> was not found.' The boundary is resource existence - the caller can no longer run a storage writer after a false update.

items.prompt: Adding a sale empties its batch, so the screen awaits addSale and then updatePigBatch with status sold_out. The second write rejects. What happens if the user retries?

choices.text: A rollback: AsyncStorage undoes the first sale automatically on failure
A duplicate sale: the first was already saved, so the retry adds a new id
No duplicate: addSale is idempotent by the sale's id, so it is skipped
A not-found error: the batch is already sold out, so the retry fails

choices: A rollback: AsyncStorage undoes the first sale automatically on failure
A duplicate sale: the first was already saved, so the retry adds a new id
No duplicate: addSale is idempotent by the sale's id, so it is skipped
A not-found error: the batch is already sold out, so the retry fails

items.explanation: The first sale was already persisted, the alert claimed it was not saved, and the retry creates a new id. Nothing spans the two AsyncStorage keys; one failure message covers two sequential writes.

items.prompt: Update now throws for a missing id. Why does deletePigBatch still silently succeed when the id is already absent?

choices.text: Because a repeated delete reaches the same end state, which is safe for retries
Because filter has no way to detect whether anything was actually removed
It is an oversight; the rubric requires delete to throw on a missing id too
Because AsyncStorage rolls back a delete whenever the stored array would be unchanged

choices: Because a repeated delete reaches the same end state, which is safe for retries
Because filter has no way to detect whether anything was actually removed
It is an oversight; the rubric requires delete to throw on a missing id too
Because AsyncStorage rolls back a delete whenever the stored array would be unchanged

items.explanation: A repeated delete expresses the same intent and reaches the same end state. Silently accepting absence on update reports success while overwriting nothing; on delete the outcome is what the user asked for.

items.prompt: replaceRecordById throws synchronously inside the async updateSale callback. What does the caller observe?

choices.text: A resolved promise, because async functions swallow synchronous throws
A rejected promise, raised before the first await, so saveSales is not reached
An uncaught exception that crashes the React Native app outright
A rejection, but one that arrives after saveSales has finished writing the sales

items.explanation: Inside an async function a throw becomes a rejection; because it happens before the await, a missing resource and a storage failure never share a success path.

items.prompt: After the change, updatePigBatch is called with an id that is not in pigBatches. What is the sequence of effects?

choices.text: The helper inserts the batch as a brand-new record, quietly turning the update into an add
savePigBatches runs first, and then the helper throws during setPigBatches
findIndex gives -1, the helper throws, and neither the save nor setState runs
The helper returns the original array, and the save is skipped as a no-op

items.explanation: Valid id: index found, new array, storage write, state update. Missing id: throw, no write, no state change.

items.prompt: A callback's closure still holds an array containing a record that was deleted since. Does the helper stop the update?

choices.text: No - the id is in the captured array, so the write resurrects the record
Yes - React refreshes callback closures before an async callback runs
Yes - the helper re-reads storage before it checks whether the id exists
No - but AsyncStorage then rejects writes that contain deleted ids

Yes - React refreshes callback closures before an async callback runs
Yes - the helper re-reads storage before it checks whether the id exists
No - but AsyncStorage then rejects writes that contain deleted ids

items.explanation: The id is present in the captured array, so the guard passes. Preventing that needs a version check or a re-read before write, not a stronger helper.

items.prompt: A call to replaceRecordById succeeds. Which claim does that establish?

choices.text: That at least one record with that id existed in the array it was given
That the caller is authorized to modify the record being replaced
That exactly one record had that id, so the replacement was unambiguous here
That the supplied array matched what is currently stored in AsyncStorage

choices: That at least one record with that id existed in the array it was given
That the caller is authorized to modify the record being replaced
That exactly one record had that id, so the replacement was unambiguous here
That the supplied array matched what is currently stored in AsyncStorage

items.explanation: It does not establish that ids are unique or that the array is the latest persisted one. Keeping exists, unique and current separate lets a reviewer tell an identity error from a persistence or concurrency error.

items.prompt: Two context callbacks holding different copies of the sales array each call saveList. What is the result?

choices.text: A throw on the second call: replaceRecordById detects the conflicting copies
The second write fails: the key is still locked by the first write
Both edits kept: AsyncStorage merges the two arrays by record id
Last writer wins: each saveList overwrites the stored collection in one setItem

choices: A throw on the second call: replaceRecordById detects the conflicting copies
The second write fails: the key is still locked by the first write
Both edits kept: AsyncStorage merges the two arrays by record id
Last writer wins: each saveList overwrites the stored collection in one setItem

items.explanation: saveList replaces the whole collection with one setItem, so the earlier write is overwritten. The helper is a local state rule, not a database transaction; whole-array writes have no concurrency control.

items.prompt: In the baseline, updatePigBatch ran pigBatches.map((item) => (item.id === batch.id ? batch : item)) and then saved. What happened when the batch id was stale?

choices.text: map returned an unchanged copy, which was saved - success reported, nothing changed
map threw a TypeError because no element matched, so the save never ran
AsyncStorage refused the write, because the serialized content was byte-identical to before
The stale batch was appended to the end of the array and then saved

choices: map returned an unchanged copy, which was saved - success reported, nothing changed
map threw a TypeError because no element matched, so the save never ran
AsyncStorage refused the write, because the serialized content was byte-identical to before
The stale batch was appended to the end of the array and then saved

items.explanation: The map returned an array equal to the original, storage was rewritten with it and the state setter accepted it. A map answers 'what would the array look like if this id were present', not 'did the resource exist'.

items.prompt: The user edits a sale whose record was deleted elsewhere. What does SaleFormScreen show?

choices.text: No message; the form navigates back as if the save had succeeded
The generic 'could not be saved. Please try again.' alert, not 'was not found'
Record '<id>' was not found. - the helper's own error text, shown verbatim
A prompt offering to re-create the deleted sale as a brand-new record

choices: No message; the form navigates back as if the save had succeeded
The generic 'could not be saved. Please try again.' alert, not 'was not found'
Record '<id>' was not found. - the helper's own error text, shown verbatim
A prompt offering to re-create the deleted sale as a brand-new record

items.explanation: The bare catch discards the helper's 'was not found' message, and retrying cannot succeed. catch without binding the error makes identity, validation and storage failures indistinguishable, and 'try again' is misleading here.

items.prompt: Why does replaceRecordById use findIndex and then map, instead of copying the array and assigning copy[index] = replacement?

choices.text: map is measurably faster than index assignment for arrays of plain objects
The baseline replaced every duplicate id; index assignment would replace one
findIndex on its own has no way to detect that the id is missing from the array
Index assignment on a copy still mutates the original array that was passed in

choices: map is measurably faster than index assignment for arrays of plain objects

items.explanation: The baseline replaced every matching id; the shortcut would replace only the first duplicate and change that contract. The change was meant to add a guard without altering behavior; test 3 (duplicate-id replacement) fails with the shortcut.

result[0] is a deep clone of a, so later edits to a do not reach it
result is [b2, a], because replaced records are moved to the front
result is a new [a, b2], and result[0] is the same object as records[0]
